A2.text:
Rashad is twenty-eight. All his life, he lived with his parents in Baku. Last month, he found his own flat and decided to move out.

The rent was not cheap, and he had to pay a big deposit. But Rashad wanted a fresh start.

First, he had to pack. His room was full of things: old books, clothes, games and papers. “I must declutter,” he said. He gave many things away and put some boxes in storage in his parents' garage.

His mother was sad. “Why do you need your own flat?” she asked. “Here you have food and clean clothes.”

On Saturday, his friends helped him carry the furniture. The new flat was small and empty. That night, Rashad felt lonely. It did not feel like home.

He opened the last box to find his towels. At the bottom, there was something soft. It was his old teddy bear from childhood! There was also a note from his mother: “So you are not alone on the first night. Mum.”

Rashad laughed and almost cried.

Slowly, he started to settle in. He bought plants and put photos on the walls. He met his neighbours. He wanted to put down roots in this place.

A month later, his mother came for dinner. She looked around and smiled. “Home sweet home,” she said.

B1.text:
At twenty-eight, Rashad was the last of his friends still living with his parents. Every evening his mother asked what time he would be home, and every morning his father commented on his shirts. So in September, he finally decided to move out.

He found a one-bedroom flat in Nasimi. The rent took a large part of his salary, and the landlord wanted a deposit of two months in advance, but Rashad didn't hesitate. He wanted a fresh start.

The hardest part was the packing. His bedroom contained twenty-eight years of life: school notebooks, football shirts that no longer fitted. He forced himself to declutter, filling six bags for charity and moving four boxes of things he couldn't throw away into storage in his parents' garage.

His mother watched all this with a face like a rainy day. “Why do you need to pay strangers when you have a room here?” she asked more than once.

On Saturday, two friends helped him carry the furniture up four flights of stairs. When they left, the flat felt huge, empty and echoing. Rashad ate a sandwich standing up, because he didn't have chairs yet, and wondered if he had made a terrible mistake.

He opened the last box to look for a towel. Underneath the towels was a familiar shape: his old brown teddy bear, missing one eye. Pinned to its ear was a note in his mother's handwriting: “For the first night, so you are not completely alone. I'm proud of you. Mum.”

He sat on the floor and laughed until his eyes were wet.

Over the next weeks, he started to settle in. He bought two chairs and a ridiculous number of plants and hung photos on the walls. For the first time, he felt he could put down roots somewhere.

When his mother finally came for dinner, she sat down at his small table. “Well,” she said, “home sweet home.” Then she took a box of dolma out of her bag.

B2.text:
At twenty-eight, Rashad held the dubious distinction of being the last of his friends still living under his parents' roof. He had a respectable job at a bank, a car, his own key — and a mother who asked every evening when he'd be back, and a father who reviewed his choice of shirt each morning like a fashion critic. In September, he finally resolved to move out.

He found a one-bedroom flat in Nasimi. The rent devoured a painful share of his salary and the landlord demanded a two-month deposit, but Rashad signed without hesitation. What he was buying, he told himself, was a fresh start.

The real ordeal was packing. His bedroom was an archaeological site containing twenty-eight years of accumulated life: exercise books from primary school, tangled headphones, football shirts two sizes too small. He made himself declutter ruthlessly, filling six bags for charity and banishing four boxes of things he couldn't bring himself to throw away to storage in his parents' garage.

His mother observed the process with an expression of quiet tragedy. “Why pay strangers,” she asked, more than once, “when you have a perfectly good room here?”

On Saturday, two friends helped him haul the furniture up four flights of stairs. When they'd gone, the flat felt cavernous and faintly hostile, every sound echoing. Rashad ate a sandwich standing at the kitchen counter, having no chairs yet, and began to suspect he had made an expensive mistake.

He opened the last box in search of a towel. Beneath the towels, wrapped in a carrier bag, lay a familiar shape: his old brown teddy bear, one eye long since lost. Pinned to its ear was a note in his mother's unmistakable handwriting: “For the first night, so you're not completely alone. I'm proud of you. Mum.”

He sat down on the bare floor and laughed until his eyes stung.

Over the following weeks, he began to settle in. He acquired two chairs and an irrational quantity of houseplants, hung photographs, and learned the names of the elderly couple across the landing. For the first time, he could imagine putting down roots.

When his mother eventually came for dinner, she toured every room, adjusted the angle of one frame and sat down at his small table. “Well,” she conceded, “home sweet home.” Then she produced, from the depths of her handbag, a container of dolma.
